title: Attackers Hide AI Prompt Injections Inside Phishing Emails
key_facts: Barracuda published research on 7 Oct 2026 analysing a phishing campaign that combined traditional social engineering with prompt injection hidden in the same message.
The email looked like internal correspondence: the From and To addresses matched, it carried a trusted spam score and came from a public-sector domain.
The email had a password-protected attachment, with the password given in the message body; opening it would lead to credential theft or malware.
Barracuda named four common hiding methods: HTML comments, invisible CSS text, Base64 data and zero-width characters.
Examples described include a hidden invoice instruction to add a fake payment-change action, and hidden resume text telling an AI screener to rate the candidate 10 out of 10.
Barracuda did not say how widespread the campaign was and said no single control stops every variation.
quote_evidence: Barracuda said it analyzed a campaign that combined traditional social engineering, such as password-protected attachments, with prompt injection concealed in the same message.
It did not say how widespread the campaign was.
why_it_matters_hint: An AI assistant that summarises an inbox could be steered by hidden text to present a phishing email as legitimate or urgent.
notes: Article read in full (fulltext file). One firm's research on one campaign; no wider count.
